sections.h2: How a Mount Laurel sale works
sections.html: A Mount Laurel sale runs through three local desks: Community Development / Construction for the Certificate of Continued Occupancy, the Tax Collector for the payoff, and the Burlington County Clerk in Mount Holly for the deed. The township is mostly owner-occupied, so most sales are between households that care about condition.

Population is about 47,738, up 7.0 percent from the 2020 base. Owners occupy 77.0 percent of housing, and the median value of an owned home is $357,200. The township has 19,657 households and a median household income of $118,802.

A rent of $2,143 set against a typical owned home worth $357,200 points to a sizable apartment and townhouse stock next to the single-family streets. Average one-way commute is 27.0 minutes.

Mount Laurel gave its name to the Mount Laurel Doctrine, the New Jersey Supreme Court's 1975 decision, reaffirmed in 1983, requiring municipalities to zone for housing that low- and moderate-income households can afford. A home with an affordable housing deed restriction follows its own resale rules, so check with the township's affordable housing staff before you pick a price.

Heating, cooling and roof condition are routine inspection topics for buyers here. The township covers 21.99 square miles, and place names you may see include Ramblewood, Rancocas Woods, Centerton, Hartford, Masonville and Fellowship.

This is a highway township. The New Jersey Turnpike runs about 7.5 miles through it, with Exit 4 leading to Route 73, while Interstate 295 has exits 36, 40 and 43. Route 38 and County Route 537 round out the local network, and NJ Transit routes 317, 413 and 457 reach Philadelphia and Camden.

Mount Laurel Schools teach pre-kindergarten through grade 8. Six neighborhood schools serve K-4: Countryside, Fleetwood, Hillside, Larchmont, Parkway and Springville. Everyone then moves to Hartford School for grades 5 and 6 and Harrington Middle School for grades 7 and 8. Lenape High School in Medford, part of the Lenape Regional High School District, takes grades 9 through 12. Since the K-4 school is set by address, an ad that names the zone speaks to families directly.

The township posts a Certificate of Continued Occupancy application and checklist under its Community Development / Construction pages, and emailed applications are not taken. Bring a paper application to the municipal building at 750 Centerton Road.

Phone the office for the current fee and the inspection calendar, then walk through the checklist on your own before the inspector arrives. Buyer attorneys often ask for the certificate, and an unmet item can push the closing date back. Landlords selling a rental should also read the township's rental ordinance and safety inspection checklist, which have a separate Landlord Information page along with rental registration.

  • Download the application and the checklist from the township page.
  • Close any open building permits before you book.
  • Check the checklist items room by room.

The Tax Collector bills in February, May, August and November, due on the first, with ten days of grace under N.J.S.A. 54:4-66. A postmark does not count, and arrears accrue 8% on the first $1,500 and 18% beyond it under N.J.S.A. 54:4-67.

The third installment shifts each year with the state's rate. When bills go out late, the township ties the due date to the mailing, 25 days from the day bills are sent. If your sale closes around August, ask the Tax Collector for the exact figure and due date before the closing statement is drawn.

The office at 750 Centerton Road accepts payment at the window, by mail, in a drop box or online. If a lender escrows your taxes, confirm that it received the bill, because a bill that never arrived is no defense against interest.

sections.h2: Deed recording costs in Burlington County
sections.html:
The Burlington County Clerk records the deed. The checklist for a recordable deed lists $45 for the first page, counting the summary sheet, and $10 per extra page, in addition to the state realty transfer fee set by the sale price.

The deed must name grantor and grantee, give the grantee's address, state the consideration and carry the municipal block and lot, a notarized signature and the seller's residency declaration. Seller tax declarations signed on or after October 1, 2025 must use the latest state form. For deeds over $1 million, the graduated percent fee in P.L. 2025, c. 69 starts at 1% and falls on the seller. Call the clerk at 609-265-5122, and consider the free Property Fraud Alert, which warns you when anything is recorded under your name.

A tidy house in a K-4 school zone with a passed CCO does well on the open market. A direct cash sale is better when the checklist looks expensive, an estate is involved, or you want a certain closing day.

  • Listing: the broadest set of buyers, with repairs and the CCO done beforehand.
  • Owner sale: no listing commission, though pricing and paperwork fall to you.
  • Cash purchase: bought in its present state, with fewer showings and a price reflecting condition.

Collect the CCO status, tax figure and payoff letter, then set each offer side by side on net proceeds.

Begin at the municipal building. Pick up the paper application, ask about fees and the inspection calendar, and learn whether any permit on your house is still open. Then go through the checklist room by room and make the fixes you can handle yourself.

While the inspection is pending, order the payoff letter from your lender and ask the Tax Collector for the current installment amount. If the house carries an affordable housing deed restriction, get the resale terms in writing from the township staff before you set a price. At closing, the attorney or title agent sends the deed to Mount Holly with the residency declaration and the recording fees.

Keep copies of the application, the checklist and any inspection notes in one folder for the buyer's attorney. A missed item found late is the usual cause of a delayed closing in a township that expects the certificate, and the fix is easier when the office already knows your file. If you live out of the area, ask whether someone you authorize can meet the inspector.

An as-is cash sale shortens the list of steps because there is no lender appraisal, but someone still has to finish the certificate items and close the permits, so settle that in the contract.

faqs.q: Does Mount Laurel Township ask for a CCO at sale?
faqs.a: Yes. The township publishes a Certificate of Continued Occupancy application and checklist, and it does not take applications by email. Call Community Development / Construction for fees and scheduling.

faqs.q: What are the installment dates for Mount Laurel taxes?
faqs.a: They fall on the first of February, May, August and November, followed by a ten-day grace period. The township does not honor postmarks.

faqs.q: What recording charges apply for a Mount Laurel deed?
faqs.a: The Burlington County Clerk lists $45 for the first page and $10 for each added page, plus the state realty transfer fee. Sales above $1 million may owe the graduated percent fee.

faqs.q: Where do Mount Laurel students attend high school?
faqs.a: Lenape High School in Medford, within the Lenape Regional High School District. The township's own district ends at grade 8.

faqs.q: Could I sell my Mount Laurel house as-is to a cash buyer?
faqs.a: Yes, an as-is sale is permitted. The CCO items and any open permits still need an owner, so ask the township and your attorney who must finish them and by when.
